docs.title: Website Development
docs.text:
Welcome to the website development lesson hub.

In these lessons, you will plan, design, build, test, and improve websites for different projects. Each project may have a different theme, audience, and purpose, but the same design process will help you make clear and useful pages.

You will learn how to:

  • Plan a website for a specific audience
  • Organise information into clear sections
  • Design wireframes before building
  • Create pages with a consistent layout
  • Test and improve your work
  • Explain the choices you made

docs.title: How to Use These Lessons
docs.text:
Work through each lesson in order. The activities will guide you from early planning to a finished website.

Most lessons include:

  • Learning intention and success criteria
  • Keywords
  • Examples
  • Levelled tasks
  • Reflection questions

Use the navigation menu to choose your current project and lesson.

docs.title: Python Outputs, Inputs and Variables
docs.text:
Learning Intention Success Criteria
  • Learn how to display outputs in Python.
  • Learn how to collect inputs from the user.
  • Understand how variables store data in a program.
  • Build simple Python programs using outputs, inputs and variables.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Use print() to display messages.
  • Use input() to ask the user questions.
  • Store information in variables.
  • Create a simple Python program using inputs and outputs.

docs.title: Today's Keywords
docs.text: Keyword Meaning Output Information displayed by a program. Input Information sent from the user to the computer. Variable A named storage place for data in a program. Value The data stored inside a variable.

docs.title: What is Python?
docs.text:
Python is a powerful programming language.

It is used to create:

  • Games
  • Websites
  • Apps
  • Data tools
  • Artificial intelligence programs

Python is popular because it is easier to read than many other programming languages.

docs.title: What is an Output?
docs.text:
An output is information displayed by the computer.

Programs use outputs to show messages, instructions, answers and results.

In Python, we display outputs using print().

Example:

print("Hello World")

This program displays the words:

Hello World

docs.title: What is an Input?
docs.text:
An input is information sent from the user to the computer.

Programs often need information from the user to work properly.

Examples of inputs:

  • Typing on a keyboard
  • Clicking a mouse
  • Speaking into a microphone
  • Tapping a touchscreen

In Python, we ask for inputs using input().

Example:

input("What is your name? ")

This program:

  1. Displays a question.
  2. Waits for the user to type an answer.

docs.title: What is a Variable?
docs.text:
A variable is a named storage place used to store data in a program.

Programs use variables to remember information.

Examples of information a program might store:

  • A player score in a game
  • A username
  • A password
  • A high score

Example:

name = "Mr Wood"

In this program:

Part Meaning name The variable name "Mr Wood" The value being stored

You can think of a variable like a labelled box that stores information.

docs.title: Combining Inputs and Variables
docs.text:
Inputs become much more useful when we store them in variables.

Example:

name = input("What is your name? ")
print(name)

docs.title: What Happens Here?
docs.text:
1. Python asks the user a question.
  2. The user types an answer.
  3. The answer is stored in the variable called name.
  4. The program displays the stored answer.

Programs become much more useful when we combine:

  • Inputs
  • Variables
  • Outputs

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Create a program that asks for the user's name and displays a greeting.

name = input("What is your name? ")

print("Hello", name)

docs.title: Step-by-Step
docs.text:
1. The program asks the user for their name.
  2. The answer is stored in the variable called name.
  3. The program displays a greeting.
  4. The stored name is displayed as part of the output.

docs.title: Programming Tasks
docs.text:
Level 1Level 2Level 3Level 4Challenge

Create a mini chatbot.

Your program should:

  • Ask the user at least four questions.
  • Store each answer in a variable.
  • Display a final message using the answers.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text:
Display the message:

Hello World

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Display three separate messages about yourself.

Your program should use three print() statements.

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text:
Ask the user for their name.

Store their answer in a variable.

Display their name back to them.

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text:
Ask the user for their favourite game.

Store their answer in a variable.

Display a sentence that includes their favourite game.

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text:
Ask the user for:

  • Their name
  • Their age

Store both answers in variables.

Display both pieces of information back to the user.

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
Ask the user for:

  • Their name
  • Their favourite food
  • Their favourite colour

Display a short sentence using all three answers.

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text:
Create a simple profile program.

Ask the user for:

  • Their name
  • Their age
  • Their favourite subject

Display the information as a short profile.

docs.title: Task 8
docs.text:
Create a simple quiz question.

Ask the user a question and store their answer in a variable.

Display their answer back to them in a sentence.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
Before moving on, make sure you can:

  • Explain the difference between an output, input and variable.
  • Use print() to display information.
  • Use input() to ask a question.
  • Store user input in a variable.
  • Combine inputs, variables and outputs in one program.

docs.title: Website Devlopment Unit 1
docs.text:
Six-lesson Third Level Computing Science unit for introducing website development with RocketCake.

Topic: Visit Edinburgh one-page website

The unit is designed for pupils to create a one-page website using RocketCake's drag-and-drop interface. Pupils should not write HTML, CSS or JavaScript. The included lesson HTML files are teacher resource pages only.

docs.title: Folder Map
docs.text:
• Scheme of Work.md - full six lesson overview
  • Teacher Guide.md - delivery notes and differentiation
  • Lessons/ - one HTML resource file per lesson
  • Resources/Questions/ - retrieval, discussion and exit questions
  • Resources/Presentations/ - slide-style lesson prompts
  • Templates/ - pupil planning, research, testing and evaluation templates
  • Assessment/ - assessment task, rubric and feedback sheets
  • Images/ - simple classroom visuals and wireframes

docs.title: Final Pupil Product
docs.text:
Each pupil or pair creates a one-page RocketCake website called Visit Edinburgh. It should include:

  • a clear title and purpose
  • at least three researched sections
  • suitable images with source notes
  • navigation links or anchors within the page if supported
  • a consistent layout
  • accessibility checks
  • testing evidence
  • a short evaluation

docs.title: Learning Intention and Success Criteria
docs.text:
Learning Intention Success Criteria
  • Plan a one-page website by identifying the audience.
  • Plan the purpose of the website.
  • Choose useful sections for the page.
  • Decide the order of the content before building.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • I can identify the target audience and the website's main purpose.
  • I can choose useful sections for a design.
  • I can explain why the section order helps the visitor.
  • I can create a clear page plan before building.

docs.title: Todays Keywords
docs.text: Keyword Meaning Audience Who the website is designed for, such as tourists, families, or first-time visitors. Purpose What the website is trying to do, such as inform, guide, persuade, or help someone plan. Section A block of related content on the page, such as attractions, transport, or visitor tips. Information The facts, details, and messages the visitor needs. Layout How text, images, headings, and sections are arranged on the page.

docs.title: Before You Plan the Page, Plan the Visitor's Journey
docs.text:
When you are designing a website you should always be thinking of the end user and asking:

Question What to Think About Who is it for? Choose a specific audience, such as families, tourists, students, or first-time visitors. What does the user need? Think about the visitor's main goal, such as planning a trip, finding attractions, or checking transport. What information comes first? Put the most useful details near the top so visitors do not have to search for them. What action should the user take? Decide whether the site guides the visitor to explore, book, contact someone, or plan their route.

Each question helps you decide what the visitor needs and how the page should be organised.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
Start at Level One then keep working through the questions.

Challenge yourself to see how far you can go.

Level OneLevel TwoLevel ThreeLevel Four

Question 1

Who is the audience for the Visit Edinburgh website?

Question 2

What is one purpose of the website?

Question 3

Name one thing tourists would need to know before visiting Edinburgh.

Question 4

Name two sections that would help tourists use the website.

Question 5

Explain why the most useful tourist information should appear near the top of the page.

Question 6

Describe how clear headings would help visitors find Edinburgh information quickly.

Question 7

Suggest the best first section for the tourist website and justify your choice.

Question 8

Explain how your section order supports tourists who need quick trip information.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
Before moving on, make sure you can:

  • Identify the audience for the Visit Edinburgh website.
  • Explain the purpose of the website.
  • Choose useful sections for a one-page website.
  • Explain why the order of the sections helps the visitor.
  • Use the keywords audience, purpose, section, information, and layout correctly.

docs.text:
Learning Intention Success Criteria
  • Learn what a wireframe is used for.
  • Plan the sections for a one-page website.
  • Decide where headings, text, and images could go.
  • Create a wireframe before building the website.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • I can explain what a wireframe is used for.
  • I can choose suitable sections for my website.
  • I can place sections in an order that helps the visitor.
  • I can add clear notes about headings, text, and images.

docs.title: Todays Keywords
docs.text: Keyword Meaning Wireframe A simple plan that shows where the main parts of a web page will go. Section A block of related content on the page, such as attractions, transport, or visitor tips. Heading A short title that tells the visitor what a section is about. Content Order The sequence that information appears in on the page. Annotation A short note added to a design to explain what should be included.

docs.title: Designing a Wireframe
docs.text:
Every website needs a clear journey and before we can start building our website we need to make a template of how it is going to look.

In Web Development this is called a Wireframe.

A wireframe does not need finished colours, fonts, or images. It is a planning tool that helps you decide what each section will contain before you start building.

When creating your wireframe, think about:

  • What the visitor needs first
  • Which sections will be most useful
  • Where headings, text, and images could go
  • How the page will guide the visitor from top to bottom

docs.title: Example Layout
docs.text:
This is one possible section order for the Visit Edinburgh website.

Section Purpose Title A strong heading and image to welcome visitors. Introduction A short overview of what the page is about. Attractions Key places to visit in Edinburgh. Transport How to get to and around the city. Visitor tips Practical advice for a better trip. Credits Sources, image credits, and extra information.

The order matters because visitors should see the most useful information before they reach smaller details such as credits.

docs.title: Wireframe Checklist
docs.text:
Before you begin, make sure your wireframe has space for:

  • A clear page title
  • A short introduction
  • At least three useful content sections
  • Notes for headings
  • Notes for text
  • Notes for images
  • Credits or source information

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
Use your answers from Task One to decide the sections, headings, and order of your website.

Start at Level One then keep working through the questions.

Challenge yourself to see how far you can go.

Level OneLevel TwoLevel ThreeLevel FourChallenge Question

Create a basic wireframe and add sections in an order that mostly makes sense.

Create a clear wireframe with suitable sections in a sensible order, with notes for headings, text, and images.

Create a detailed wireframe and add well-chosen sections in a logical order that guides the visitor.

Create a complete wireframe and add all key sections in the best order, with clear notes so someone else could build the page.

Justify your section order by linking it to the audience's needs.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
Before moving on, make sure you can:

  • Explain what a wireframe is.
  • Describe why a wireframe is useful before building.
  • Choose suitable sections for a Visit Edinburgh website.
  • Explain why your section order helps the visitor.
  • Add clear notes so someone else could understand your design.

Pupils submit:

Teacher assessment uses the rubric in Assessment/Rubric.md.

docs.text: Lesson Focus Main Outcome Evidence 1 What makes a useful website? Pupils analyse audience, purpose and page structure Website brief and page plan 2 Information and research Pupils gather and organise content for a one-page site Research log and asset log 3 Building the first version Pupils use RocketCake to create page sections and add content Draft website 4 Layout, navigation and representation Pupils improve structure, readability and device suitability Improved layout and navigation 5 Testing, accessibility and refinement Pupils test against requirements and fix issues Test plan and changes 6 Final assessment and evaluation Pupils submit and explain final website decisions Final site and evaluation

docs.title: Suggested Topic Requirements
docs.text:
The Visit Edinburgh page should include at least three of:

  • Edinburgh Castle
  • Royal Mile
  • National Museum of Scotland
  • Arthur's Seat
  • public transport
  • food and family activities
  • accessibility information
  • safety and visitor tips

docs.title: Big Idea
docs.text: This unit introduces website development through design choices, information structure, audience needs and testing. RocketCake is used so pupils can focus on computational thinking, representation and evaluation without writing code.

docs.title: Key Vocabulary
docs.text:

  • one-page site

  • navigation
  • browser

  • packet

docs.title: Delivery Notes
docs.text:
• Keep the pupil product to one page.
  • Pupils should not hand-code HTML, CSS or JavaScript.
  • Model RocketCake tools live: text, images, containers, links, preview and responsive/device view.
  • Encourage pupils to cite sources for text and images.
  • When discussing mark-up, keep it conceptual: webpages have structure behind the scenes, but pupils are using a visual editor.

docs.title: Differentiation
docs.text:
Support:

  • provide the section headings in advance
  • use the sentence starters in the templates
  • reduce required sections from four to three
  • pair pupils strategically

Challenge:

  • add anchor-style navigation if available in RocketCake
  • compare desktop and mobile layout
  • improve accessibility with alt text, contrast and readable headings
  • explain how browser requests and packets are involved in loading the page

docs.title: Misconceptions
docs.text:
• A website and webpage are not always the same. This unit creates one webpage within a website project.
  • Images from the internet are not automatically free to use.
  • A colourful page is not always a useful page.
  • Testing is not just checking whether the page opens. It checks requirements, readability and user needs.

docs.title: Slide 1: Title
docs.text:
Kicker: Lesson 01 Title: Planning a One Page Website Subtitle: Decide who the website is for, what it should do, and how the page should be organised.

Purpose: Introduce the unit project: pupils will plan and later build a one-page "Visit Edinburgh" website.

docs.title: Slide 2: Learning Intention and Success Criteria
docs.text:
Learning intention: We will plan a one-page website by identifying the audience, purpose, sections, and content order.

Success criteria: - I can identify the target audience and the website's main purpose. - I can choose useful sections for a one-page design. - I can explain why the section order helps the visitor. - I can create a clear page plan before building.

docs.title: Slide 3: Key Words
docs.text:
Kicker: Key Words Title: Words we will use today

Keyword cards:

Audience Who the website is designed for, such as tourists, families, or first-time visitors.

Purpose What the website is trying to do, such as inform, guide, persuade, or help someone plan.

Section A block of related content on the page, such as attractions, transport, or visitor tips.

Layout How text, images, headings, and sections are arranged on the page.

Information The facts, details, and messages the visitor needs.

Footer prompt: Use these words when explaining your page plan.

docs.title: Slide id = "06"
docs.text:
Kicker: Website Questions Title: Before you plan the page, plan the visitor's journey

Context: When you are designing a website you first need to understand what the visitor needs and how the page should be organised.

Try to think like a person who will visit your website: what do they need first, next, and last?

You should always consider the following questions:

Question cards:

Who is it for? Choose a specific audience, such as families, tourists, students, or first-time visitors.

What does the user need? Think about the visitor's main goal, such as planning a trip, finding attractions, or checking transport.

What information comes first? Put the most useful details near the top so visitors to your website do not have to search for them.

What action should the user take? Decide whether the site guides the visitor to explore, book, contact someone, or plan their route.

Side note: Use your answers to decide the sections, headings, and order of your one-page website.

docs.title: Slide 5: Example Layout
docs.text:
Kicker: Wireframes Title: A website always needs a clear journey

Structure list: 1. Title - A strong heading and image to welcome visitors. 2. Introduction - A short overview of what the page is about. 3. Attractions - Key places to visit in Edinburgh. 4. Transport - How to get to and around the city. 5. Visitor tips - Practical advice for a better trip. 6. Credits - Sources, image credits, and extra information.

Image: Assets/Images/wireframe-one-page.svg

Footer prompt: Plan the order first, then build each section with a clear purpose.

docs.title: Slide 6:
docs.text:
Kicker: Task One Title: Choose the level that stretches your thinking

You are planning a one-page "Visit Edinburgh" website for tourists who want to quickly find useful trip information.

1 - Beginning to learn - Who is the audience for the "Visit Edinburgh" website? - What is one purpose of the website?

2 - Making progress - Give one thing tourists would need to know before visiting Edinburgh. - Name two sections that would help tourists use the website.

3 - Making good progress - Explain why the most useful tourist information should appear near the top of the page. - Describe how clear headings would help visitors find Edinburgh information quickly.

4 - Meeting target - Suggest the best first section for the tourist website and justify your choice. - Explain how your section order supports tourists who need quick trip information.

Footer prompt: Start where you feel confident, then try the next level.

Kicker: Task two Title: Create the wireframe for your 'Visit Edinburgh Website'

Task steps: 1. Open Powerpoint 1. Think about the sections your page needs. 2. Using shapes to draw rectangles, circles etc put the sections of your webpage into a logical order. 3. Add notes about headings, text, images, and useful details. 4. Add a print scren of your work to your workbook

Support: Use the sentence starter: "My website is for ___ and it helps them by ___."

Challenge: Justify your section order by linking it to the audience's needs.

docs.title: Slide 8: Exit Ticket
docs.text:
Kicker: Exit Ticket Title: Explain your page idea

1 - Beginning to learn Complete: My website is for ___.

2 - Making progress Complete: My website is for ___ and it helps them by ___.

3 - Making good progress Complete: My website is for ___ and its purpose is to ___ because ___.

4 - Meeting target Complete: My website is for ___ and its purpose is to . My first section is ___ because ___ and this supports users by .

Final takeaway: Audience is who the website is for. Purpose is what the website is trying to do.

docs.title: Lesson 02 Presentation: Research and Information Models
Slide 1: Title
docs.text:
Kicker: Lesson 02 Title: Research and Information Models Subtitle: Turning facts into useful website content

Purpose: Introduce the lesson focus and connect research to the one-page website pupils planned in Lesson 01.

docs.title: Slide 2: Learning Intention and Success Criteria
docs.text:
Learning intention: We will gather reliable information and organise it into a simple information model for a one-page website.

Success criteria: - I can collect useful facts from suitable sources. - I can record where text and images came from. - I can describe each content item using clear characteristics. - I can explain how an information model helps visitors compare information.

Footer prompt: Reliable research makes the website more useful for real visitors.

docs.title: Slide 3: Key Words
docs.text:
Kicker: Key Words Title: Words we will use today

Keyword cards:

Source Where information or an image came from, such as a website, guide, map, or official page.

Reliable Information that is accurate, trustworthy, and suitable for the task.

Information model A structured way to describe real-world things using the same set of fields.

Characteristic A detail that describes an item, such as name, location, category, cost, or visitor value.

Credit A note showing where text, images, or information came from.

Footer prompt: Use these words when explaining how you chose your website content.

docs.title: Slide 4: Research Questions
docs.text:
Kicker: Research Questions Title: Before you collect content, check that it is useful

Context: You are researching content for a one-page "Visit Edinburgh" website. Your audience is tourists who want useful trip information quickly.

Question cards:

Is the source suitable? Check whether the website is relevant, current, and likely to be trustworthy.

What fact is useful? Choose information a visitor would actually need, not just anything interesting.

Can I rewrite it? Record facts in your own words so your page sounds clear and original.

What credit is needed? Save the website name, URL, and image credit so sources can be acknowledged.

Side note: Good research is not collecting everything. It is choosing what helps the visitor.

docs.title: Slide 5: Information Model
docs.text:
Kicker: Information Model Title: Describe each attraction in the same way

Context/scenario: You are collecting attractions or visitor topics for the website. Each item should use the same fields so it can be compared, sorted, or searched later.

Suggested model fields:

Field What it records Example Name What the item is called Edinburgh Castle Category The type of item Attraction Description A short visitor-friendly summary Historic castle near the Royal Mile Location Where it is Castlehill Visitor value Why it helps the audience Good for history and views Source Where the fact came from Official visitor website Image credit Where the image came from Website or photographer credit

Footer prompt: An information model helps us describe real-world information clearly.

docs.title: Slide 6: Sorting and Searching
docs.text:
Kicker: Computing Link Title: Models make information easier to use

Context: If every attraction uses the same fields, the information can be organised in useful ways.

Examples:

Sort by name Put attractions into alphabetical order so users can scan them quickly.

Sort by category Group attractions, transport, food, and visitor tips.

Search by location Find items near the Royal Mile, city centre, or a transport route.

Compare visitor value Decide which items best match the audience's needs.

Side note: Structured information is easier to sort, search, compare, and reuse.

docs.title: Slide 7: Your Task
docs.text:
Kicker: Main Task Title: Build your research log

Task steps: 1. Choose at least three attractions or visitor topics for the "Visit Edinburgh" website. 2. Find useful facts from suitable sources. 3. Rewrite each fact in your own words. 4. Record the source name and URL. 5. Record image sources or credits. 6. Complete the information model fields for each item.

Support: Use the sentence starter: "This section is useful for visitors because..."

Challenge: Choose one field that could be used for sorting or searching and explain why.

docs.title: Slide 8: Check for Understanding
docs.text:
Kicker: Check for Understanding Title: Choose the level that stretches your thinking

Scenario: You are creating an information model for Edinburgh attractions that tourists could use to compare places quickly.

1 - Beginning to learn - What is an information model? - Name one detail you could collect about an attraction.

2 - Making progress - Give three characteristics to describe a tourist attraction. - Put three attractions into alphabetical order.

3 - Making good progress - Explain one way attractions could be sorted. - Explain one way attractions could be searched.

4 - Meeting target - Design a simple information model for attractions and explain why your fields are useful. - Explain how your model helps users compare attractions quickly.

Footer prompt: Start where you feel confident, then try the next level.

docs.title: Slide 9: Exit Ticket
docs.text:
Kicker: Exit Ticket Title: What did your research prove?

1 - Beginning to learn Name one source you used.

2 - Making progress Name one source and one fact from it.

3 - Making good progress Name one source and rewrite one fact in your own words.

4 - Meeting target Name one source, rewrite one fact in your own words, and justify why the source is trustworthy.

Final takeaway: A strong website starts with reliable information organised in a clear model.

docs.text:

  • Use context-scenario for the scaffolded question scenario on Slide 8.
  • Use clear side-note/footer classes where the slide needs guidance text.
  • Keep each slide to one viewport where possible.
  • Use keyword-card styling for Slide 3.
  • Use question-list style for Slide 4.
  • Use a table or card-based model layout for Slide 5.
  • Use the four-level question table pattern for Slide 8 and Slide 9.

docs.title: Slide 1: Title
docs.text:
Kicker: Lesson 03 Title: Building in RocketCake Subtitle: Turn the plan into the first version of a one-page website.

Purpose: Move pupils from planning and research into practical website construction using RocketCake's visual tools.

docs.title: Slide 2: Learning Intention and Success Criteria
docs.text:
Learning intention: We will use RocketCake to build the first version of a one-page website from a plan.

Success criteria: - I can create and save a new RocketCake project. - I can add headings, text, images, and content sections. - I can preview my page and compare it with my plan. - I can make build decisions that support my audience and purpose.

Footer prompt: Build one section at a time: heading, image, short paragraph, useful detail.

docs.title: Slide 3: Key Words
docs.text:
Kicker: Key Words Title: Words we will use today

Keyword cards:

Visual development tool Software that lets you build a page by arranging objects rather than writing all the code by hand.

Container A layout area that holds related content, such as a heading, image, and paragraph.

Preview Viewing the page as a user would see it in a browser or preview window.

Draft An early version of the website that can still be improved.

Consistency Using repeated styles, spacing, and structure so the page feels organised.

Footer prompt: Use these words when explaining how you built your first version.

docs.title: Slide 4: RocketCake Tools
docs.text:
Kicker: RocketCake Tools Title: Choose the right tool for each part of the page

Context: You are building the first draft of your "Visit Edinburgh" website. Each tool should help you create the page planned in Lesson 01.

Question/tool cards:

New project Start a clean website file and save it with a clear project name.

Text and headings Add the title, introduction, section headings, and short visitor-friendly paragraphs.

Image Insert suitable images that match your researched content and audience.

Container Group related information so each section feels organised and easy to scan.

Preview and save Check the page often and save regularly so progress is not lost.

Side note: The tool is not the goal. The goal is a clear page that matches the plan.

docs.title: Slide 5: Build Order
docs.text:
Kicker: Build Order Title: Build from the plan, not from memory

Suggested order: 1. Create the project and save it. 2. Add the page title and short introduction. 3. Build section 1 from the storyboard. 4. Build section 2 from the storyboard. 5. Build section 3 from the storyboard. 6. Add image credits and source notes. 7. Preview the whole page.

Footer prompt: Following the plan helps your page stay organised.

docs.title: Slide 6: Good Habits
docs.text:
Kicker: Good Habits Title: Small checks stop big problems later

Habit cards:

Save often Save after every major change so you do not lose work.

Preview often Check how the page looks before adding more content.

Use your plan Build the sections in the order you planned.

Keep spacing consistent Similar sections should feel like they belong to the same website.

Use meaningful content Text and images should help the visitor, not just fill space.

Side note: Good builders check as they go.

docs.title: Slide 7: Your Task
docs.text:
Kicker: Main Task Title: Create the first draft website

Task steps: 1. Create a new RocketCake project called Visit Edinburgh. 2. Add the page title and short introduction. 3. Create at least three content sections from your plan. 4. Add at least one suitable image. 5. Preview the page and compare it with your storyboard. 6. Save the project.

Support: Build one section at a time: heading, image, short paragraph, useful detail.

Challenge: Create a consistent section style so the page feels organised.

docs.title: Slide 8: Check for Understanding
docs.text:
Kicker: Check for Understanding Title: Choose the level that stretches your thinking

Scenario: You have started building the "Visit Edinburgh" page in RocketCake and need to check that the draft still matches your plan.

1 - Beginning to learn - Which RocketCake tool adds text? - Which RocketCake tool adds images?

2 - Making progress - Describe how to add a heading and a paragraph. - Describe how to place an image in the correct section.

3 - Making good progress - Explain how layout choices can improve readability. - Explain why consistent spacing matters.

4 - Meeting target - Evaluate your current page against your plan and identify one precise improvement. - Explain how your build decisions support the target audience.

Footer prompt: Start where you feel confident, then try the next level.

docs.title: Slide 9: Exit Ticket
docs.text:
Kicker: Exit Ticket Title: What did you build today?

1 - Beginning to learn Name one thing you added today.

2 - Making progress Name two changes you made today.

3 - Making good progress Name two changes and explain why they improved your page.

4 - Meeting target Name two changes, explain why they improved your page, and link each change to audience or purpose.

Final takeaway: RocketCake helps you build visually, but the plan should still guide every decision.

docs.title: Lesson 04 Presentation: Layout, Navigation and Devices
Slide 1: Title
docs.text:
Kicker: Lesson 04 Title: Layout, Navigation and Devices Subtitle: Improve structure, readability, and how the page works for different users.

Purpose: Help pupils refine the draft website so information is easier to understand and navigate.

docs.title: Slide 2: Learning Intention and Success Criteria
docs.text:
Learning intention: We will improve the structure and readability of a one-page website and check how it appears on different devices.

Success criteria: - I can improve headings, spacing, and section order. - I can explain how layout affects user understanding. - I can preview the page on different device sizes. - I can make navigation choices that support the audience.

Footer prompt: Good layout helps visitors understand the page quickly.

docs.title: Slide 3: Key Words
docs.text:
Kicker: Key Words Title: Words we will use today

Keyword cards:

Heading A clear label that tells users what a section is about.

Whitespace Empty space around content that helps the page feel readable and organised.

Navigation How users move through the website or find the section they need.

Device The screen used to view the page, such as a phone, tablet, laptop, or desktop monitor.

Responsive layout A layout that changes or adapts so the same information can be used on different screens.

Footer prompt: Use these words when explaining how your layout helps users.

docs.title: Slide 4: Structured Information
docs.text:
Kicker: Structured Information Title: Headings and sections help users scan the page

Context: Your one-page website has several sections. Visitors should be able to understand what each section is for without reading everything first.

Question cards:

Are headings clear? Each heading should tell the user what information comes next.

Are sections grouped well? Related text, images, and facts should sit together.

Is spacing consistent? Similar sections should have similar spacing so the page feels organised.

Can users scan quickly? Important information should be easy to find without searching through long paragraphs.

Side note: Structure makes information easier to understand.

docs.title: Slide 5: Devices
docs.text:
Kicker: Device Preview Title: The same webpage can look different on different screens

Context/scenario: Your website might be viewed on a phone, tablet, laptop, or desktop monitor. The content is the same, but the layout may change.

Comparison points:

Phone Content may stack vertically and images may take up more screen height.

Tablet Some sections may fit side by side, but spacing still needs checking.

Desktop There is more horizontal space, but wide lines of text can become harder to read.

Footer prompt: Previewing helps you spot layout problems before users do.

docs.title: Slide 6: Navigation
docs.text:
Kicker: Navigation Title: One-page websites still need a clear route

Navigation checks: - Does the first section introduce the page clearly? - Does the section order match the visitor's needs? - Would anchor links or a section menu help? - Are credits and sources easy to find? - Does the page ending feel complete?

Side note: Navigation is not only menus. It is also the order and clarity of the page.

docs.title: Slide 7: Your Task
docs.text:
Kicker: Main Task Title: Improve the layout and preview the page

Task steps: 1. Check that every section has a clear heading. 2. Improve spacing between sections. 3. Make images and text easier to read. 4. Preview the page on at least two device sizes. 5. Improve one part of the navigation or section order. 6. Record what changed and why it helped the user.

Support: Choose one section and improve only its heading, spacing, and image placement first.

Challenge: Compare the page on two devices and justify one layout improvement for your audience.

docs.title: Slide 8: Check for Understanding
docs.text:
Kicker: Check for Understanding Title: Choose the level that stretches your thinking

Scenario: You are reviewing your Visit Edinburgh page on different devices and deciding which layout changes will help visitors most.

1 - Beginning to learn - What does a browser do? - Name one part of a web address.

2 - Making progress - Give two ways the same information could be represented on a webpage. - Define sender and receiver.

3 - Making good progress - Explain sender, receiver, address, and packets in simple terms. - Explain how these ideas relate to loading your webpage.

4 - Meeting target - Explain how structured information and network processes both affect user experience. - Evaluate one navigation choice in your page and justify whether it should stay or change.

Footer prompt: Start where you feel confident, then try the next level.

docs.title: Slide 9: Exit Ticket
docs.text:
Kicker: Exit Ticket Title: What changed and why did it help?

1 - Beginning to learn Describe one layout change you made.

2 - Making progress Describe one layout change and why you made it.

3 - Making good progress Describe one layout change and explain how it helped readability.

4 - Meeting target Describe one layout change and evaluate its impact on users on different devices.

Final takeaway: The same information can be represented differently depending on layout, device, and user need.

docs.text:
• Use the existing presentation template design system.
  • Use keyword-card styling for Slide 3.
  • Use question-list style with question-context for Slide 4 and Slide 6.
  • Use a comparison/table or image-content layout for Slide 5.
  • Use the four-level question table pattern with context-scenario for Slide 8 and Slide 9.

docs.title: Slide 1: Title
docs.text:
Kicker: Lesson 05 Title: Testing and Refinement Subtitle: Use evidence and feedback to improve the final website.

Purpose: Help pupils test their website, collect useful feedback, and make justified improvements.

docs.title: Slide 2: Learning Intention and Success Criteria
docs.text:
Learning intention: We will test a one-page website, use feedback, and refine it to improve usability and accessibility.

Success criteria: - I can test my website against requirements. - I can identify readability, link, image, and accessibility issues. - I can use peer feedback to choose improvements. - I can explain how a change improved the user experience.

Footer prompt: Testing is useful when it leads to a specific improvement.

docs.title: Slide 3: Key Words
docs.text:
Kicker: Key Words Title: Words we will use today

Keyword cards:

Testing Checking whether the website works, meets the brief, and is suitable for users.

Accessibility Designing so more people can read, understand, and use the website.

Feedback Information from another person that helps the designer improve the work.

Refinement A change made to improve the quality of the website.

Evidence Proof that a test was carried out or an improvement was made.

Footer prompt: Use these words when explaining your improvements.

docs.title: Slide 4: Types of Test
docs.text:
Kicker: Testing Questions Title: Choose tests that reveal useful problems

Context: You are testing the first draft of your Visit Edinburgh website before final submission.

Question cards:

Does it meet the brief? Check whether the page is one page, about Visit Edinburgh, and suitable for the chosen audience.

Is it readable? Check headings, text size, spacing, contrast, and whether paragraphs are easy to scan.

Do links and images work? Check that links open correctly and images display clearly with suitable credits.

Is it accessible? Check image descriptions, contrast, clear language, and whether information is easy to understand.

Side note: Good testing finds problems you can actually fix.

docs.title: Slide 5: Accessibility
docs.text:
Kicker: Accessibility Title: More users can use a page when the design is clear

Checks: - Clear headings show what each section is about. - Text is readable and not too small. - Colours have enough contrast. - Images have useful descriptions or credits. - Important information is not hidden in long paragraphs. - The page still makes sense on different devices.

Footer prompt: Accessible design is good design.

docs.title: Slide 6: Feedback
docs.text:
Kicker: Feedback Title: Specific feedback leads to better refinements

Context: A peer is testing your website. Their feedback should help you decide what to improve next.

Useful feedback examples:

Specific "The transport section needs a clearer heading."

Linked to users "Tourists might need opening times near the top."

Actionable "Increase the contrast on this paragraph."

Evidence-based "This link did not open when I clicked it."

Side note: "It is good" is kind, but it does not tell the designer what to improve.

docs.title: Slide 7: Your Task
docs.text:
Kicker: Main Task Title: Test, collect feedback, and refine

Task steps: 1. Complete a test plan for your website. 2. Test readability, links, images, spelling, and accessibility. 3. Ask a peer to test your website. 4. Record feedback and evidence. 5. Choose at least two refinements. 6. Make the changes and check that they worked.

Support: Use the structure: issue, evidence, fix, retest.

Challenge: Prioritise the most important issue and justify why fixing it matters for the user.

docs.title: Slide 8: Check for Understanding
docs.text:
Kicker: Check for Understanding Title: Choose the level that stretches your thinking

Scenario: You have tested your Visit Edinburgh website and found several possible improvements.

1 - Beginning to learn - Give one test for readability. - Give one test for images.

2 - Making progress - Describe one way to test links. - Describe what to do after finding an error.

3 - Making good progress - Explain the difference between identifying an issue and fixing an issue. - Explain how you would prioritise multiple errors.

4 - Meeting target - Create a mini test checklist and justify the order. - Evaluate one change made from peer feedback and explain its impact.

Footer prompt: Start where you feel confident, then try the next level.

docs.title: Slide 9: Exit Ticket
docs.text:
Kicker: Exit Ticket Title: What evidence shows your website improved?

1 - Beginning to learn Name one issue you found.

2 - Making progress Name one issue and how you fixed it.

3 - Making good progress Name one issue, how you fixed it, and how you checked the fix worked.

4 - Meeting target Name one issue, explain your fix, and evaluate how the change improved accessibility or usability.

Final takeaway: Testing is strongest when it creates evidence for a real refinement.

docs.text:

  • Use keyword-card styling for Slide 3.
  • Use question-list style with question-context for Slide 4 and Slide 6.
  • Use a checklist/table layout for Slide 5.
  • Use the four-level question table pattern with context-scenario for Slide 8 and Slide 9.

docs.title: Lesson 06 Presentation: Final Assessment and Evaluation
Slide 1: Title
docs.text:
Kicker: Lesson 06 Title: Final Assessment and Evaluation Subtitle: Submit the website and explain how well it meets the brief.

Purpose: Guide pupils through final checks, submission evidence, rubric thinking, and reflective evaluation.

docs.title: Slide 2: Learning Intention and Success Criteria
docs.text:
Learning intention: We will submit a final one-page website and evaluate it using evidence from planning, building, testing, and refinement.

Success criteria: - I can complete final checks before submission. - I can identify evidence that shows my website meets the brief. - I can evaluate strengths and areas for improvement. - I can link design decisions to audience, purpose, and user experience.

Footer prompt: A strong evaluation uses evidence, not just opinion.

docs.title: Slide 3: Key Words
docs.text:
Kicker: Key Words Title: Words we will use today

Keyword cards:

Evaluation Judging the quality of the final website using evidence.

Evidence Proof from planning, research, testing, screenshots, feedback, or the final product.

Success criteria The points used to judge whether the work has met the task.

Refinement A change made to improve the website after testing or feedback.

Next step Something that could be improved in a future version.

Footer prompt: Use these words when explaining the quality of your final website.

docs.title: Slide 4: Evidence
docs.text:
Kicker: Evidence Title: What proves the website meets the brief?

Context: You are preparing to submit your Visit Edinburgh website. You need evidence from across the project, not just the final page.

Evidence cards:

Planning Website brief, audience, purpose, storyboard, and section order.

Research Research log, source notes, image credits, and information model.

Website The final one-page RocketCake website with clear content and layout.

Testing Test plan, peer feedback, issues found, fixes made, and retest evidence.

Evaluation A written judgement explaining strengths, improvements, and next steps.

Side note: Evidence helps you prove that the final website did not happen by accident.

docs.title: Slide 5: Rubric
docs.text:
Kicker: Rubric Title: What will quality look like?

Assessment areas:

Area What to look for Design Layout, readability, section order, and visual consistency Content Useful information for the audience and clear source awareness Technical use Effective use of RocketCake tools Testing Evidence of checks, feedback, fixes, and retesting Evaluation Clear judgement linked to evidence Computing understanding Audience, purpose, structured information, and user experience

Footer prompt: The rubric shows what to evidence, not just what to finish.

docs.title: Slide 6: Strong Evaluation
docs.text:
Kicker: Evaluation Title: Explain decisions using evidence

Context: Your evaluation should show what worked, what changed, and what you would improve next.

Evaluation prompts:

Strength What works well in the final website? What evidence proves this?

Decision Which design choice helped the audience or purpose?

Refinement What did you change after testing or feedback?

Next step What would you improve if you had more time?

Side note: Avoid "I like it" on its own. Explain what works and why.

docs.title: Slide 7: Your Task
docs.text:
Kicker: Final Task Title: Submit and evaluate

Task steps: 1. Complete final checks on the website. 2. Make sure sources and image credits are included. 3. Save/export/submit the final website as instructed. 4. Gather evidence from planning, research, building, and testing. 5. Write an evaluation using the success criteria. 6. Identify one realistic next step.

Support: Use: "One strength is ___ because the evidence shows ___."

Challenge: Evaluate whether your evidence is strong enough and identify any gaps.

docs.title: Slide 8: Check for Understanding
docs.text:
Kicker: Check for Understanding Title: Choose the level that stretches your thinking

Scenario: You are evaluating your final Visit Edinburgh website and deciding what evidence proves its quality.

1 - Beginning to learn - Name one strength of your website. - Name one target for improvement.

2 - Making progress - Match one piece of evidence to one success criterion. - Choose one computing word that explains your design work.

3 - Making good progress - Explain how one piece of evidence demonstrates quality. - Explain how your testing improved the final version.

4 - Meeting target - Evaluate whether your evidence is sufficient and identify any gaps. - Justify one improvement target for a future project.

Footer prompt: Start where you feel confident, then try the next level.

docs.title: Slide 9: Exit Ticket
docs.text:
Kicker: Exit Ticket Title: What would you improve next time?

1 - Beginning to learn Complete: Next time I would improve ___.

2 - Making progress Complete: Next time I would improve ___ because ___.

3 - Making good progress Complete: Next time I would improve ___ because . I would do this by .

4 - Meeting target Complete: Next time I would improve ___ because . I would do this by . This would improve user experience by ___.

Final takeaway: Evaluation helps you explain the quality of your work and how you would improve future projects.
